en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-mahāvaipulya-bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ki-carya of the Western Regions during the Yuan-Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly.

The assembly consisted of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattvas, whose names were: Bodhisattva Jñānaketu, Dharmaketu, Candraketu, Sūryaketu, Anantaketu, and the sixteen virtuous men (satpuruṣa) headed by Bhadrapāla; the sixty like-minded ones headed by Mañjuśrī; and all the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa headed by Maitreya Bodhisattva.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, and knelt with his right knee on the ground. Scattering various precious flowers over the Buddha, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"I wish to ask something; I only pray that the World-Honored One will reveal and explain it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Good son! If you have any doubts or difficulties, ask whatever you wish; the Tathāgata shall explain them for you according to your questions, so as to bring you joy.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anantajñāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! Regarding the bodhicitta— World-Honored One,
as for what is called the bodhicitta, how should one understand the accomplishment of the bodhicitta by a bodhisattva?”

What is this so-called bodhicitta, which is neither bodhicitta nor the absence of bodhicitta, wherein neither a sentient being (sattva) can be apprehended nor is it separate from awakening (bodhi), yet is called bodhicitta?
Bodhi, moreover, cannot be spoken of, cannot be seen, and is without counterpart; even a *sattva* cannot be apprehended.
How, then, can one attain understanding regarding these dharmas?
The World-Honored One said:
"Good son! Awakening (bodhi) is entirely a matter of verbal expression, conventional designation, and conceptual construction."
"Noble son! Awakening is not verbal expression, not conventional designation, and not a conceptual construct. Noble son!"
Just as awakening (*bodhi*) is beyond verbal expression, so too are the sentient being (*sattva*) and the mind present in all phenomena; one should understand it in this way.
If such a mind exists, it is called the bodhicitta. Awakening is neither past, future, nor present; likewise, the sentient being and the mind are also neither past, future, nor present.
If one knows in this manner, then the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended, for therein nothing at all can be found.
To attain non-attainment regarding all phenomena is called attaining the bodhicitta.
Just as an arhat and the fruit of arhatship are themselves unattainable— wherein there is absolutely nothing attained, existing only as conventional designations and verbal expressions—
to have no attainment regarding all phenomena is what is meant by "attainment."
The bodhicitta is also not the initial practice; "Bodhisattva" is a designation for the meaning of "one who brings beings across.

Furthermore, that mind is neither a mind nor a designation of a mind; it is neither a sentient being nor a designation of a sentient being; it is neither a śrāvaka nor a designation of a śrāvaka; it is neither a pratyekabuddha nor a designation of a pratyekabuddha; it is neither a bodhisattva nor a designation of a bodhisattva; it is neither conditioned nor a designation of conditioned phenomena; it is neither unconditioned nor a designation of unconditioned phenomena; and it is not something that can be attained, has been attained, or will be attained.
However, because it accords with the teaching of the Dharma, it is said that all roots of goodness arise from it.
One should know that the initial arousal of the mind has its cause in the *dānapāramitā*, being like the great earth that supports all;
one should know that the arising of the second mind has its cause in the *śīlapāramitā*, being as courageous as the lion, the king of beasts.
One should know that when the third mind arises, it is due to the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, like the courageous and great power of Nārāyaṇa;
one should know that when the fourth mind arises, it subdues all fetters and enemies, due to the *vīrya-pāramitā*, as the flowers of various roots of goodness and merit bloom;

one should know that when the fifth mind arises, it is like the *kovidāra* tree at the assembly of Śakra, Lord of Devas, due to the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, like the immeasurable radiance of the solar disc.

One should know that when the sixth mind arises, it is able to completely eliminate all darkness; this is because, through the *prajñāpāramitā*, the merits of his original vows manifest everywhere as adornments.

One should know that when the seventh mind arises, he is like a leader of merchants who can guide the merchants across the wilderness; this is because, through the *upāyakauśalyapāramitā*, he purifies all faults and evils so that his aspirations are fulfilled at will.
One should know that when the eighth mind arises, it is perfectly clear and pure, just as the full autumn moon fulfills all wishes.

One should know that when the ninth mind arises, all activities come to rest; it is like a poor person finding an inexhaustible treasure trove, or like space, free from defilement and luminously pure.

One should know that when the tenth mind arises, one reaches the ultimate shore of all merits; with inexhaustible wisdom and eloquence, one becomes a sovereign of all dharmas, like a wheel-turning monarch.
In this way, noble son,
one who accomplishes these ten kinds of mind is called a bodhisattva, a mahāsattva, a foremost sattva, a supreme sattva, a sin-free sattva, and a most venerable sattva.
Nevertheless, son of good family!
In the ultimate sense, both the bodhisattva and the mind are utterly unapprehendable.
Furthermore, son of good family!
When the Bodhisattva first arouses the mind, there arises the samādhi called "Arising of the Dharma Jewel," which engenders the grasping of the mind;
when the Bodhisattva arouses the second mind, there arises the samādhi called "Immovable," which engenders the grasping of the mind;
when that third mind is aroused, it is named the samādhi called "Well-Abiding," which engenders the grasping of the mind.
That fourth mind arises, born from the grasping of the samādhi named Non-Retrogression;
that fifth mind arises, born from the grasping of the samādhi named Gathering Flowers;
that sixth mind arises, born from the grasping of the samādhi named Sunlight.
That seventh mind arises, born from the apprehension of the samādhi named Fulfillment of Name and Meaning;
that eighth mind arises, born from the apprehension of the samādhi named Torch of Wisdom;
that ninth mind arises, born from the apprehension of the samādhi named Vision of the Buddha Standing Before One.
When that tenth mind arises, it is called the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*, born from the gathering of the mind.
Furthermore, son of good family,

when a bodhisattva of the first stage first beholds auspicious omens, hundreds of thousands of millions of wondrous and rare jewel-treasuries within the trichiliocosm all appear within his field of perception.
In the second stage, as a prior auspicious omen, the great trichiliocosm of Buddha-fields appears level like the palm of a hand, manifesting its entire realm.
In the third stage, as a prior auspicious omen, valiant and sturdy figures holding weapons appear, manifesting their entire realm.
In the fourth stage, as a prior auspicious omen, mandāra winds come from the four directions, blowing various flowers that scatter everywhere across the great earth, manifesting their entire realm.

In the fifth stage, as a prior auspicious omen, one sees all women adorned with ornaments, their heads decorated with *campaka* garlands, *mokṣa* garlands, *utpala* garlands, and *vārṣika* garlands; this entire scene appears before them.

In the sixth stage, as a prior auspicious omen, one sees bathing pools made of various jewels, filled with water of eight virtues, having four stairways with golden sand spread upon their bottoms, clear, tranquil, and transparent; one sees oneself sporting within them, and this entire scene appears before them.

In the seventh stage, as a prior auspicious omen, one sees on both sides great hells of bitter torment and perilous steepness, and sees oneself emerging from these calamities; this entire scene appears before them.

In the eighth stage, as a prior auspicious omen, one sees upon one's own two shoulders the lion, king of beasts, its head crowned with silken cloth, its body majestic and powerful, subduing all venomous and malevolent wild beasts without exception—all of which appear within the field of experience.

In the ninth stage, as a prior auspicious omen, one sees a Wheel-Turning Sage King, a great minister, and a kṣatriya, along with hundreds of thousands of retinues, transforming and guiding all sentient beings through the Dharma; holding silken canopies and adorned with hundreds of thousands of various jewels upon their heads—all of which appear within the field of experience.

In the tenth stage, as a prior auspicious omen, one sees oneself becoming a Buddha, with a golden-hued body and a halo extending one fathom, surrounded by billions of Brahmās who listen to the preaching of the Dharma.
"Good son! These are the preliminary signs of the ten stages of a bodhisattva; you should know them thus, for they all arise from the samādhis of the ten stages."
"Furthermore, noble son!
A bodhisattva attains the dhāraṇī of the Most Victorious State in the stage of the initial resolve;
in the second stage, they attain the dhāraṇī of the Unconquerable."
In the third stage, one attains the dhāraṇī of "Excellent Abiding";
in the fourth stage, one attains the dhāraṇī of "Difficult to Overcome";
and in the fifth stage, one attains the dhāraṇī of "Universal Array of the Flowers of Merit."
In the sixth stage, one attains the *dhāraṇī* of the Radiance of Wisdom;
in the seventh stage, one attains the *dhāraṇī* of the Supreme Path;
in the eighth stage, one attains eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇīs*, with the *dhāraṇī* of Serene Clarity as the foremost.
In the ninth stage, one attains sixty *nayuta* of *dhāraṇīs*, with the *inexhaustible dhāraṇī* as the foremost;
in the tenth stage, one attains *dhāraṇīs* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with the *dhāraṇī that gives birth to the immeasurable* as the foremost.
These are the *dhāraṇīs* of the ten stages of the Bodhisattva; they should be understood in this way.

"Furthermore, noble son! A bodhisattva fulfills the dāna-pāramitā in the stage of initial resolve; fulfills the śīla-pāramitā in the second stage; fulfills the kṣānti-pāramitā in the third stage; fulfills the vīrya-pāramitā in the fourth stage; fulfills the dhyāna-pāramitā in the fifth stage; fulfills the prajñā-pāramitā in the sixth stage; fulfills the upāya-pāramitā in the seventh stage; fulfills the praṇidhāna-pāramitā in the eighth stage; fulfills the bala-pāramitā in the ninth stage; and fulfills the jñāna-pāramitā in the tenth stage.
Thus, these various pāramitās are all fully accomplished within their respective stages."
"Furthermore, son of good family, there are ten kinds of *dānapāramitā*.

What are the ten? They are: the *dānapāramitā* headed by the faculty of faith; the *dānapāramitā* headed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the *dānapāramitā* headed by great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*); the *dānapāramitā* headed by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); the *dānapāramitā* headed by the aspiration of the profound mind; the *dānapāramitā* headed by omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); the *dānapāramitā* headed by establishing sentient beings [in the Dharma]; the *dānapāramitā* headed by the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); the *dānapāramitā* headed by protecting and upholding the true Dharma; and the *dānapāramitā* headed by joyfully seeking the Buddha-Dharma."
"Furthermore, there are ten kinds of śīla-pāramitā. What are these ten? They are:

the śīla-pāramitā headed by the departure from the eight difficult conditions; the śīla-pāramitā headed by the establishment of the Buddha-dharma; the śīla-pāramitā headed by the transcendence of the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha; the śīla-pāramitā headed by the purification of bodily action; the śīla-pāramitā headed by the purification of verbal action; the śīla-pāramitā headed by the purification of mental action; the śīla-pāramitā headed by the adornment of the mind; the śīla-pāramitā headed by the purification of the world of humans; the śīla-pāramitā headed by the fulfillment of all aspirations and requests; and the śīla-pāramitā headed by non-harming."
“Furthermore, there are ten kinds of kṣāntipāramitā. What are these ten? They are: the kṣāntipāramitā that takes the power of patience as its primary focus;

the kṣāntipāramitā that takes the maturation of sentient beings as its primary focus; the kṣāntipāramitā that takes mental resolve as its primary focus; the kṣāntipāramitā that takes profound dharmakṣānti as its primary focus; the kṣāntipāramitā that takes the severing of afflictions as its primary focus; the kṣāntipāramitā that takes the departure from malice as its primary focus; the kṣāntipāramitā that takes the non-conceptualization of the body as its primary focus; the kṣāntipāramitā that takes the non-conceptualization of life as its primary focus; the kṣāntipāramitā that takes the severing of all ignorance as its primary focus; and the kṣāntipāramitā that takes the contemplation of the equality of all phenomena as its primary focus.”
"Furthermore, there are ten kinds of vīryapāramitā. What are these ten?

The perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) has the faculty of vigor as its foremost; the perfection of vigor has the power of vigor as its foremost; the perfection of vigor has equal skillful means as its foremost; the perfection of vigor has the foundations of mindfulness as its foremost; the perfection of vigor has acting on behalf of all sentient beings as its foremost; the perfection of vigor has conforming to the speech and minds of all sentient beings as its foremost; the perfection of vigor has non-retrogression as its foremost; the perfection of vigor has extreme diligence as its foremost; the perfection of vigor has subduing all afflictions and enemies as its foremost; and the perfection of vigor has the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (sarvajñājñāna) as its foremost.
“Furthermore, there are ten kinds of dhyānapāramitā. What are these ten? The dhyānapāramitā that takes the faculty of concentration as its primary focus;

the dhyānapāramitā that takes the power of concentration as its primary focus; the dhyānapāramitā that takes equanimity of concentration as its primary focus; the dhyānapāramitā that takes the various meditative absorptions and liberations as its primary focus; the dhyānapāramitā that takes wholesome dharmas as its primary focus; the dhyānapāramitā that takes the appropriate occasion as its primary focus; the dhyānapāramitā that takes non-distraction as its primary focus; the dhyānapāramitā that takes the inappropriate occasion as its primary focus; the dhyānapāramitā that takes the destruction of all fetters and latent tendencies as its primary focus; and the dhyānapāramitā that takes the fulfillment of the concentrated body as its primary focus.”
“Furthermore, there are ten kinds of *prajñāpāramitā*. What are these ten? They are:

the *prajñāpāramitā* headed by the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*); the *prajñāpāramitā* headed by the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*); the *prajñāpāramitā* headed by right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*); the *prajñāpāramitā* headed by right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*); the *prajñāpāramitā* headed by skillful means regarding the aggregates (*skandha*); the *prajñāpāramitā* headed by the contemplation of the elements and sense-bases (*dhātu-āyatana*); the *prajñāpāramitā* headed by the noble truths (*āryasatya*); the *prajñāpāramitā* headed by non-obstruction; the *prajñāpāramitā* headed by the removal of all false views; and the *prajñāpāramitā* headed by the endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).”
“Furthermore, there are ten kinds of skillful means wisdom *pāramitās*. What are these ten? They are: the skillful means *pāramitā* that takes the aspiration of sentient beings as its primary focus;

the skillful means *pāramitā* that takes the establishment of sentient beings as its primary focus; the skillful means *pāramitā* that takes great compassion as its primary focus; the skillful means *pāramitā* that takes tireless transformation of sentient beings as its primary focus; the skillful means *pāramitā* that takes transcending the stages of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* as its primary focus; the skillful means *pāramitā* that takes entering all the *pāramitās* as its primary focus; the skillful means *pāramitā* that takes the contemplation of all phenomena as they truly are as its primary focus; the skillful means *pāramitā* that takes inconceivable power as its primary focus; the skillful means *pāramitā* that takes non-retrogression as its primary focus; and the skillful means *pāramitā* that takes the subduing of all Māras as its primary focus.”
"What is the meaning of *pāramitā*?
The meaning of the fulfillment of progressive practice is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
the fulfillment of sublime wisdom is the meaning of *pāramitā*."
The meaning of not being attached to conditioned or unconditioned phenomena is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
the meaning of awakening to the faults of birth and death is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
the meaning of awakening those who have not yet awakened is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
The meaning of revealing the treasury of all inexhaustible dharmas is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
the meaning of being fully endowed with unimpeded and uninterrupted liberation is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
the meaning of awakening to the equality of giving is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
To realize the meaning of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, wisdom, and equanimity is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
to possess the meaning of definitive skillful means is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
to know the meaning of the *dharmatā* of all sentient beings is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
The meaning of fulfilling the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena is the meaning of pāramitā;
the meaning of fulfilling the stage of non-retrogression is the meaning of pāramitā;
the meaning of adorning and purifying the buddha-fields is the meaning of pāramitā.
The meaning of maturing sentient beings is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
the meaning of perfecting the site of awakening is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
the meaning of subduing all māras is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
The meaning of the fulfillment of all Buddha-dharmas is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
the meaning of the fulfillment of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities is the meaning of *pāramitā*;
the meaning of gathering in all those born through transformation is the meaning of *pāramitā*.
“The meaning of the Wheel of Dharma with its three turnings and twelve aspects is the meaning of the *pāramitās*.
At that time, there was a deity in the assembly named Lion Banner Unobstructed Radiance who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How truly marvelous! How truly extraordinary!
This is called the perfection of all things; this is called the ultimate fulfillment of all the merits of the Buddha-dharma.
Thus the World-Honored One replied.
"So it is, so it is, O devas!
Any son of good family or daughter of good family who hears this Dharma and correctly recollects it should be known as an *avaivartika* bodhisattva."
Why is this? O Devaputra!
Because the roots of goodness of these sons and daughters of good family have matured, their faculty of hearing is enabled to hear this sutra.

Because all their roots of goodness have reached maturity, once they have heard this sutra, they shall never be separated from the contemplation of reality, nor from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; nor shall they be separated from the teachings of the Buddhas, nor from the turning of the wheel of Dharma; nor shall they be separated from the Sea-Seal Dhāraṇī, nor from the Inexhaustible Dhāraṇī, nor from the Dhāraṇī of Pervasive Entry into the Conduct of Sentient Beings, nor from the Inexhaustible Radiance Sun-Banner Dhāraṇī, nor from the Moon-Stainless Mark Dhāraṇī, nor from the Stainless Arising-Mark Dhāraṇī.

If a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they are able at once to transform their body into that of a Buddha, pervading the ten directions to teach and transform sentient beings; yet, regarding all phenomena, they neither die nor depart as they liberate sentient beings.

Sentient beings cannot be apprehended, and the various words and letters used to preach the Dharma and provide instruction likewise cannot be apprehended. They manifest birth and death, yet are not born; they know that all phenomena are equal, without going or coming, because they neither act nor do not act.
When this Dharma was being taught, three thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven! If there are those who read, recite, and uphold this Dharma, they shall never be separated from the *dhāraṇī* that pacifies all entanglements; they shall never be separated from the *dhāraṇī* of adamantine hardness that shatters the mountains of all afflictions; they shall never be separated from the *dhāraṇī* that explains the ineffable and universally enters all *pāramitās*; they shall never be separated from the *dhāraṇī* that can express various names, phrases, and utterances; they shall not be separated from the *dhāraṇī* of the birth of the inexhaustible seal, which is stainless like space; and they shall not be separated from the *dhāraṇī* that accomplishes the bodies of immeasurable Buddhas and exhausts all births."

When this Dharma was being taught, immeasurable sentient beings all attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), and immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, the Devaputra Siṃhadhvaja-asaṅgaprabhāsa, along with the great śrāvakas, devas, humans, and asuras, prostrated before the Buddha and were all filled with great joy.
The Mahāvaipulya Bodhisattva-daśabhūmika Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha
